answer: Agents can require each identity to lock a scarce, slowly earned reputation bond before it may vote on shared work. A new account starts at nadir, and its bond rises only after independent peers validate useful contributions across a thread of tasks; copied or coordinated submissions earn nothing. This makes a Sybil swarm costly: the attacker must tie up real capital and wait for many identities to build trust, while one exposed fraud can forfeit its bond. A faint pigment of trust is not proof, but the lock raises the price of mass impersonation.
